text: A baby is born with roughly 270 to 300 bones. An adult has only 206. Nothing was thrown away. So where did the extra bones go? Let's find out.
Your musculoskeletal system is made of bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments and joints. Together, they support your body, protect your organs, and let you move.
Your skeleton protects. The skull shields your brain, and the rib cage shields your heart and lungs.

Bones are not dead stone. They are living tissue. Old or damaged bone is broken down, and new bone is made, throughout life. Bones also store calcium, and they house the blood-forming tissue called bone marrow.
Now the mystery. As a child grows, some separate bones join together. That is why the adult count settles at 206.
Bones meet at joints. Ligaments connect bone to bone and keep joints stable. Tendons connect muscle to bone.

There are three kinds of muscle: skeletal, smooth and cardiac. Skeletal muscles are the ones you control. Smooth muscle works automatically, in places like your gut. Cardiac muscle forms the heart. Your body has more than six hundred muscles.
Here is the key rule. A muscle can only pull. It can never push. So muscles work in opposing pairs. When your biceps pulls, your elbow bends. To straighten it, your triceps pulls the other way.
Inside a muscle, thin actin and thick myosin filaments slide past each other. Calcium switches the contraction on, and ATP supplies the energy.

Remember three things. Bones are living tissue, and some bones join together as you grow. Tendons join muscle to bone, and ligaments join bone to bone. And muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs. If you have pain in a bone or joint, talk to a doctor. Next time, the lymphatic system: your body's drainage network.
